title: Multi-Cloud: Azure & GCP Fundamentals
summary: AWS, Azure, and GCP offer equivalent core services under different names and with different trade-offs. Every DevOps engineer works across multiple clouds — either because their employer uses one, or because they're deploying to customers who use different clouds. This lesson maps AWS concepts to Azure and GCP equivalents, covers each cloud's managed Kubernetes service (EKS/AKS/GKE), and introduces multi-cloud patterns and tooling that works across all three.

sections.title: AWS vs Azure vs GCP: the core services map
sections.body:
**The three hyperscalers — different names, same concepts:**

```
Category          AWS                    Azure                  GCP
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Compute
  VMs             EC2                    Virtual Machines       Compute Engine
  Containers      ECS / Fargate          Container Instances    Cloud Run
  Kubernetes      EKS                    AKS                    GKE
  Serverless      Lambda                 Functions              Cloud Functions
  PaaS            Elastic Beanstalk      App Service            App Engine

Storage
  Object          S3                     Blob Storage           Cloud Storage
  Block           EBS                    Managed Disks          Persistent Disk
  File            EFS                    Azure Files            Filestore
  Archive         S3 Glacier             Archive Blob           Cloud Storage Coldline

Database
  Relational      RDS (PostgreSQL/MySQL)  Azure Database         Cloud SQL
  Managed PG      Aurora PostgreSQL       Flexible Server        AlloyDB
  NoSQL           DynamoDB               Cosmos DB              Firestore / Bigtable
  Cache           ElastiCache (Redis)     Azure Cache for Redis  Memorystore
  Data Warehouse  Redshift               Synapse Analytics      BigQuery

Networking
  VPC             VPC                    Virtual Network (VNet) VPC
  DNS             Route 53               Azure DNS              Cloud DNS
  CDN             CloudFront             Azure CDN / Front Door  Cloud CDN
  Load Balancer   ALB / NLB              Application Gateway     Cloud Load Balancing
  Private Link    PrivateLink            Private Endpoint        Private Service Connect
  Peering         VPC Peering            VNet Peering           VPC Peering

Identity & Security
  IAM             IAM                    Azure AD / Entra ID    Cloud IAM
  Secrets         Secrets Manager        Key Vault              Secret Manager
  Certificate     ACM                    Key Vault Certs        Certificate Manager
  OIDC workloads  IRSA (IAM Roles SA)    Workload Identity      Workload Identity

CI/CD & DevOps
  Registry        ECR                    ACR                    Artifact Registry
  CI/CD           CodePipeline           Azure DevOps           Cloud Build
  GitOps          CodeCommit             Azure Repos            Cloud Source Repos

Observability
  Metrics         CloudWatch             Azure Monitor          Cloud Monitoring
  Logs            CloudWatch Logs        Log Analytics          Cloud Logging
  Tracing         X-Ray                  Application Insights   Cloud Trace
```

**Key differences in philosophy:**

```
AWS:    Largest service catalog (~250 services), most mature, most complex IAM
        Best for: breadth, enterprise compliance, migration from on-prem

Azure:  Deep Microsoft integration (Active Directory, Office 365, Visual Studio)
        Best for: Microsoft shops, hybrid cloud (Azure Arc), enterprise Windows

GCP:    Best networking (global VPC, premium tier routing), best data services
        Kubernetes-native (Google invented it), best price/performance for
        compute. Best for: Kubernetes workloads, data/ML, startups
```

sections.title: Azure core services for DevOps
sections.body:
**Azure resource model — everything is inside a Resource Group:**

```
Azure Subscription
  └── Resource Group (logical container — like an AWS account/region bucket)
        ├── Virtual Network
        ├── Virtual Machines
        ├── AKS Cluster
        ├── Storage Account
        └── Key Vault

# AWS analogy: Resource Group ≈ VPC + loose grouping of resources
# GCP analogy: Resource Group ≈ Project
```

**Azure CLI — equivalent to AWS CLI:**

```bash norun
# Login
az login

# Set active subscription
az account set --subscription "My Subscription"

# Create a resource group (required before creating anything)
az group create --name myapp-rg --location eastus

# AKS — Azure Kubernetes Service
az aks create \
  --resource-group myapp-rg \
  --name myapp-cluster \
  --node-count 3 \
  --node-vm-size Standard_D2s_v3 \
  --enable-managed-identity \
  --enable-oidc-issuer \
  --enable-workload-identity \
  --generate-ssh-keys

# Get kubeconfig
az aks get-credentials --resource-group myapp-rg --name myapp-cluster

# Azure Container Registry
az acr create \
  --resource-group myapp-rg \
  --name myappregistry \
  --sku Basic

# Attach ACR to AKS (grants AKS pull access)
az aks update --name myapp-cluster --resource-group myapp-rg \
  --attach-acr myappregistry
```

**Azure Workload Identity — pods authenticate to Azure services without secrets:**

```yaml
# Equivalent to AWS IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts)
# The pod gets a managed identity, no long-lived credentials needed

apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    # Azure AD application client ID
    azure.workload.identity/client-id: "<MANAGED_IDENTITY_CLIENT_ID>"
labels:
  azure.workload.identity/use: "true"
```

**Azure Key Vault + CSI Driver — mount secrets as files:**

```yaml
# SecretProviderClass — maps Key Vault secrets to pod files
apiVersion: secrets-store.csi.x-k8s.io/v1
kind: SecretProviderClass
metadata:
  name: azure-kvname
spec:
  provider: azure
  parameters:
    usePodIdentity: "false"
    useVMManagedIdentity: "true"
    keyvaultName: "myapp-keyvault"
    objects: |
      array:
        - |
          objectName: db-password
          objectType: secret
    tenantId: "<TENANT_ID>"
```

**Azure Blob Storage (equivalent to S3):**

```bash norun
# Create storage account
az storage account create \
  --name myappstorage \
  --resource-group myapp-rg \
  --sku Standard_LRS \
  --kind StorageV2

# Create a container (equivalent to S3 bucket)
az storage container create \
  --account-name myappstorage \
  --name artifacts

# Upload a file
az storage blob upload \
  --account-name myappstorage \
  --container-name artifacts \
  --name myfile.tar.gz \
  --file ./myfile.tar.gz
```

sections.title: GCP core services for DevOps
sections.body:
**GCP resource hierarchy — Projects, not accounts:**

```
Organization (company.com)
  └── Folder (optional grouping)
        └── Project  ← the billing and IAM boundary (like an AWS account)
              ├── GKE Cluster
              ├── Cloud Storage buckets
              ├── Cloud SQL instances
              └── Artifact Registry

# AWS analogy: GCP Project ≈ AWS Account
# The project is also the IAM boundary — permissions are per-project
```

**gcloud CLI:**

```bash norun
# Login
gcloud auth login

# Set project
gcloud config set project my-project-id

# GKE — Google Kubernetes Engine (the best managed k8s)
gcloud container clusters create myapp-cluster \
  --zone us-central1-a \
  --num-nodes 3 \
  --machine-type e2-standard-2 \
  --enable-workload-identity \
  --workload-pool=my-project-id.svc.id.goog

# Get kubeconfig
gcloud container clusters get-credentials myapp-cluster --zone us-central1-a

# Artifact Registry (successor to Container Registry)
gcloud artifacts repositories create myapp \
  --repository-format=docker \
  --location=us-central1

# Tag and push an image
docker tag myapp:latest \
  us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/myapp/myapp:latest
docker push us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/myapp/myapp:latest
```

**GCP Workload Identity — pods use service accounts without key files:**

```yaml
# Bind a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to a GCP Service Account
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp
  namespace: production
  annotations:
    iam.gke.io/gcp-service-account: myapp@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com
```

```bash norun
# Allow the k8s SA to impersonate the GCP SA (IAM binding)
gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding \
  myapp@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --role roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser \
  --member "serviceAccount:my-project.svc.id.goog[production/myapp]"
```

**GCP Secret Manager:**

```bash norun
# Create a secret
echo -n 'my-db-password' | gcloud secrets create db-password --data-file=-

# Access from a pod (using Application Default Credentials via Workload Identity)
python3 -c "
from google.cloud import secretmanager
client = secretmanager.SecretManagerServiceClient()
name = 'projects/my-project/secrets/db-password/versions/latest'
response = client.access_secret_version(request={'name': name})
print(response.payload.data.decode('UTF-8'))
"
```

**BigQuery — GCP's data warehouse (no AWS/Azure equivalent):**

```bash norun
# BigQuery is unique: serverless SQL on petabyte scale, no infrastructure to manage
bq query --use_legacy_sql=false \
  'SELECT COUNT(*) as total, status
   FROM my_project.analytics.requests
   WHERE DATE(timestamp) = CURRENT_DATE()
   GROUP BY status'

# Process a TB of data in seconds — you only pay for the data scanned
```

sections.title: Multi-cloud patterns and cloud-agnostic tooling
sections.body:
**Cloud-agnostic tooling — write once, run anywhere:**

```
Terraform    → infrastructure provisioning across all three clouds
             AWS provider:   registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/aws
             Azure provider: registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/azurerm
             GCP provider:   registry.terraform.io/hashicorp/google

Helm         → same charts deploy on EKS, AKS, GKE
             Cloud-specific values in values-aws.yaml, values-azure.yaml, etc.

ArgoCD       → works on any k8s cluster regardless of cloud
External Secrets → supports AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, GCP Secret Manager
Cert-manager → supports Let's Encrypt, Vault, all cloud CAs
Crossplane   → provision cloud resources from Kubernetes CRDs
```

**Terraform multi-cloud pattern:**

```hcl
# Use workspaces or separate state files per cloud
# backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket = "mycompany-tfstate"
    key    = "aws/production/terraform.tfstate"
    region = "us-east-1"
  }
  required_providers {
    aws   = { source = "hashicorp/aws",     version = "~> 5.0" }
    azurerm = { source = "hashicorp/azurerm", version = "~> 3.0" }
    google = { source = "hashicorp/google",  version = "~> 5.0" }
  }
}

# Abstract cloud-specific resources with modules
module "k8s_cluster" {
  source = "./modules/k8s-cluster"
  cloud  = var.cloud   # "aws" | "azure" | "gcp"
  ...
}
```

**External Secrets Operator — unified secret management:**

```yaml
# Same ESO CRD works across all clouds — only the SecretStore changes

# AWS:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: us-east-1

# Azure:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
spec:
  provider:
    azurekv:
      vaultUrl: https://my-vault.vault.azure.net

# GCP:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: SecretStore
spec:
  provider:
    gcpsm:
      projectID: my-project-id
```

**Multi-cloud cost comparison (approximate, 2026):**

```
Resource              AWS              Azure            GCP
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2 vCPU, 8GB RAM      t3.large $0.083/h D2s_v3 $0.096/h  e2-standard-2 $0.067/h
Managed PostgreSQL   db.t3.medium      General Purpose   db-standard-2
  (2vCPU, 4GB)       $0.068/h          $0.13/h           $0.104/h
Object storage       S3 $0.023/GB      Blob $0.018/GB    GCS $0.020/GB
Managed k8s (mgmt)   EKS $0.10/h       AKS Free          GKE $0.10/h
Egress (first 10TB)  $0.09/GB          $0.087/GB         $0.08/GB

Conclusion: GCP typically 10-20% cheaper for compute; Azure for Microsoft shops;
AWS for the widest service catalog and enterprise compliance needs.
```

**When to go multi-cloud:**

```
Good reasons:
  - Customer requirement: "we only allow data in Azure"
  - Avoid vendor lock-in on managed services
  - Disaster recovery across providers
  - Best-of-breed: GCP for ML (Vertex AI), AWS for compliance, Azure for AD integration

Bad reasons:
  - "We should hedge against a cloud going down" (all three have 99.9%+ uptime)
  - Premature: multi-cloud doubles operational complexity before you've mastered one
  - Cost arbitrage: savings rarely justify the complexity

Recommendation: master one cloud deeply first, then expand.
```

sections.title: Exercise: map AWS commands to Azure and GCP equivalents
sections.body:
Practice the CLI equivalents across clouds without needing live cloud accounts — using the local cluster as context.

```bash norun
# ── 1. Explore the cluster's cloud-agnostic resources ────────────────────
# External Secrets Operator is already installed. Check the SecretStore:
kubectl get secretstore -A
kubectl describe secretstore -n learning

# ── 2. Examine the ExternalSecret for DB credentials ─────────────────────
kubectl get externalsecrets -A
kubectl describe externalsecret -n learning

# ── 3. Review the Terraform structure for cloud-agnostic patterns ─────────
cat << 'EOF'
# This pattern works across all three clouds:
# - Same Kubernetes manifests (Deployment, Service, Ingress)
# - Same Helm charts
# - Same ArgoCD application
# Only the SecretStore provider changes per cloud

# AWS:
# provider.aws.service: SecretsManager

# Azure:
# provider.azurekv.vaultUrl: https://my-vault.vault.azure.net

# GCP:
# provider.gcpsm.projectID: my-project-id
EOF

# ── 4. Compare managed Kubernetes CLI commands ────────────────────────────
cat << 'EOF'
# ── EKS (AWS) ──
# Create cluster:
# eksctl create cluster --name prod --region us-east-1 --nodes 3
# Get kubeconfig:
# aws eks update-kubeconfig --name prod --region us-east-1

# ── AKS (Azure) ──
# Create cluster:
# az aks create -g myapp-rg -n prod --node-count 3
# Get kubeconfig:
# az aks get-credentials -g myapp-rg -n prod

# ── GKE (GCP) ──
# Create cluster:
# gcloud container clusters create prod --zone us-central1-a --num-nodes 3
# Get kubeconfig:
# gcloud container clusters get-credentials prod --zone us-central1-a
EOF

# ── 5. Practice cloud-agnostic secret access pattern ─────────────────────
# Create a secret the 'cloud-agnostic' way using ESO
kubectl create secret generic simulated-backend-store \
  --from-literal=api-key=cloud-agnostic-demo-key \
  -n learning 2>/dev/null || true

# Apply an ExternalSecret that reads from the fake store
kubectl apply -n learning -f - << 'YAML'
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1beta1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: cloud-demo-secret
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef:
    name: local-store
    kind: SecretStore
  target:
    name: cloud-demo-secret
    creationPolicy: Owner
  data:
  - secretKey: api-key
    remoteRef:
      key: simulated-backend-store
      property: api-key
YAML

# ── 6. Review what k8s resources are cloud-agnostic ──────────────────────
kubectl api-resources | grep -E 'Deployment|Service|Ingress|HPA|PDB'
# All of these work identically on EKS, AKS, and GKE

# ── 7. Clean up ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
kubectl delete externalsecret cloud-demo-secret -n learning 2>/dev/null || true
kubectl delete secret simulated-backend-store cloud-demo-secret -n learning 2>/dev/null || true
```

questions.q: What is the GCP equivalent of AWS S3 object storage?
questions.explanation: Google Cloud Storage is the GCP equivalent of AWS S3. Like S3, it provides durable, scalable object storage with multiple storage classes (Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive). The Azure equivalent is Azure Blob Storage.

questions.q: What is the AWS IAM equivalent on Azure for a pod needing to access cloud resources without storing credentials?
options: Azure Managed Identity with Workload Identity federation
questions.explanation: Azure Workload Identity (using Managed Identities) is the Azure equivalent of AWS IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). A Kubernetes ServiceAccount is annotated with a managed identity client ID, and AKS uses OIDC federation to allow the pod to authenticate to Azure services without any stored credentials.

questions.q: Which tool provides a unified interface for provisioning resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP?
questions.explanation: Terraform has providers for all major cloud platforms and uses a single HCL language to describe infrastructure across clouds. The AWS, Azure, and GCP providers are all maintained by HashiCorp. Helm handles Kubernetes application packaging (cloud-agnostic at the k8s layer), but Terraform handles the underlying cloud infrastructure.

sections.title: Challenge: design a multi-cloud deployment
sections.goal: Design and document a deployment strategy for a web application that needs to run on both AWS and Azure, sharing the same Kubernetes manifests but with cloud-specific secret management and container registries.
hints: Start by listing what differs per cloud (registry URL, SecretStore provider, IAM annotations) vs what stays the same (Deployment, Service, HPA, NetworkPolicy)
Use Helm values files to handle cloud differences: `values-aws.yaml` and `values-azure.yaml`
External Secrets Operator's SecretStore is the only resource that needs to change — ExternalSecret and the app manifests stay identical
For the container registry: use `imageRegistry` as a Helm value — `aws_account.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/myapp` vs `myregistry.azurecr.io/myapp`
success_criteria: A Helm chart exists with a `values.yaml`, `values-aws.yaml`, and `values-azure.yaml`
The chart uses `imageRegistry` and `secretStore.provider` as configurable values
Two SecretStore manifests exist (one for each cloud provider) in separate overlays or value files
The core Deployment, Service, and HPA are identical between both cloud configurations
A README explains how to deploy to each cloud: `helm install ... -f values-aws.yaml` vs `values-azure.yaml`
